MHT has co-developed and implemented Heat Action Plans in collaboration with local governments across six cities, integrating community-led, climate-responsive solutions. These plans are designed to protect low-income communities, informal workers, and other at-risk groups, by enhancing preparedness and resilience to extreme heat. Jodhpur Heat Action Plan In 2023, Jodhpur Nagar Nigam North, MHT, and NRDC jointly published a hyper-local Heat Action Plan that introduced a ward-level Heat Vulnerability Index, identifying 22 high-risk wards targeting housing improvements, livelihood protections, early warning systems, access to cooling infrastructure, and strengthening institutional coordination. Jalgaon Heat Action Plan This Heat Action Plan for Jalgaon has been developed by the Jalgaon City Municipal Corporation (JCMC) in collaboration with Mahila Housing Trust (MHT) through a participatory and multi-stakeholder process. The plan integrates inputs from key stakeholders, including various departments of JCMC, institutes, community women leaders, and civil society organisations. View Jalgaon Heat Action Plan Indore Heat Action Plan To strengthen Indore’s preparedness for rising temperatures and the growing impacts of climate change, Mahila Housing Trust (MHT), in collaboration with the H T Parekh Foundation and Indore Municipal Corporation (IMC), launched the Women-Led Inclusive Heat Action Plan for Indore. The plan was formally launched by Shri Arth Jain, CEO, Indore Smart City, and Additional Commissioner (Transport), Indore Municipal Corporation. MHT served as the key knowledge partner in developing the plan, which provides a structured, sustained, and forward-looking framework to strengthen heat resilience across the city’s departments and wards. View Heat Action Plan Jaipur Heat Action Plan This Heat Action Plan has been developed for the Jaipur Nagar Nigam by Mahila Housing Trust through a collaborative process, integrating inputs from key stakeholders including Jaipur Nagar Nigam, departments of the Rajasthan State Government, community leaders, and civil society organisations. View Heat Action Plan Varanasi Heat Action Plan On May 16, 2025, Varanasi Nagar Nigam, in partnership with the Department of Medical Health & Family Welfare, Mahila Housing Trust (MHT), NRDC, and IIPHG, launched the Varanasi Heat Action Plan (HAP)—a locally rooted, scientifically informed initiative designed to protect communities from rising extreme heat. This data-driven, equity-focused plan is tailored to Varanasi’s unique climate challenges and community needs. It features ward-level heat vulnerability mapping, future climate projections, community-led interventions, and special attention to high-footfall areas like ghats and informal settlements. The launch event highlighted insights from MHT, NRDC, and IIPHG, along with an MoU signing and strong commitments from municipal and district leadership. From cool roofs in dense settlements to crowd-sensitive public health measures at major ghats, the plan prioritizes communities at every step. Download the Varanasi Heat Action Plan . When orange and red flags are raised, Ahmedabad takes several measures to cool off the city, for instance, opening cooling facilities in community centers, providing people with water and pill drinks, changing the working hours of outdoor workers, and boosting public health surveillance. The city sets its targets on the most vulnerable groups of people including the elderly, informal workers employed outdoors, and homeless. Jalgaon’s Community-Centered Implementation Jalgaon, a smaller city in Maharashtra, has developed community-centered heat action planning supported by the University of Toronto India Foundation and Mahila Housing Trust. Rather than purely top-down municipal approaches, Jalgaon’s plan emphasizes community knowledge and participation. The plan maps vulnerable neighborhoods and populations through community engagement. Heat vulnerability assessments identify households most at risk. Community health workers, trusted local authorities deliver heat safety messaging and check on vulnerable residents. Cooling centers incorporate community input on location, timing, and services offered. Jalgaon’s approach demonstrates that effective city heat action plan implementation in India requires community partnership rather than exclusive municipal delivery. Residents know their neighborhoods best; incorporating their knowledge improves targeting and acceptance. Implementation Challenges Despite progress, city heat action plan implementation India faces substantial barriers. Vulnerable populations often lack awareness of cooling centers or are hesitant to use them due to stigma or access challenges. Outdoor workers, construction laborers, informal transport operators, street vendors, often cannot cease work despite dangerous conditions given economic necessity. Healthcare systems struggle with surge capacity during extreme heat events. Financing green infrastructure proves difficult for resource-constrained municipalities. Additionally, heat waves’ increasing frequency and intensity outpace adaptation. Plans developed for historical heat patterns become inadequate as climate change intensifies. Updating plans requires recognizing that heat management is not a temporary response to temporary problems but a permanent feature of urban management requiring sustained commitment. Research and Knowledge Gaps The University of Toronto India Foundation or UTIF is providing support to research that studies the implementation of plans that combat heat in cities in India and tries to determine what measures work best in reaching vulnerable segments of the population, as well as how to develop the capacity of institutions for sustained implementation. Workshops aim to increase capacity of ULBs and NGOs in planning for and responding to effects of high temperatures through knowledge exchange and driving data-driven decision making. Research-based approaches will help municipalities ensure that applied approaches are both effective and based on tested solutions. Frequently Asked Questions Q: How can residents protect themselves during heat waves if their city lacks a formal heat action plan? A: Even without formal municipal planning, individuals can take protective measures: stay hydrated, limit outdoor activity during peak heat hours (11am-4pm), seek shade and air-conditioned spaces, check on elderly and vulnerable neighbors, modify exercise timing, wear light-colored loose clothing, and monitor health for heat-related illness symptoms (dizziness, nausea, headache). Communities can advocate for municipal heat action planning while implementing individual and neighborhood-level protection. Q: How much does it cost cities to implement heat action plans? A: Costs vary substantially. Early warning systems and cooling centers require modest infrastructure investment (INR 1-5 crores depending on city size). Green infrastructure investment (tree planting, cool roofs, permeable pavements) can cost INR 100+ crores for comprehensive programs. However, avoided healthcare costs, reduced mortality, and improved productivity often exceed implementation costs. Many cities implement phased approaches beginning with low-cost interventions (early warning, cooling centers) before larger infrastructure investments. Q: Which Indian cities have the most comprehensive heat action plans? A: Ahmedabad leads with longest-established, most systematic planning. Jalgaon demonstrates community-centered approaches. Pune, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Mumbai are developing plans of varying maturity. However, most Indian cities lack comprehensive heat action plans, representing significant vulnerability. Expansion to all major cities represents urgent priority. Q: How do heat action plans address outdoor workers particularly vulnerable to heat exposure? A: Effective plans establish work schedules allowing cessation or reduced activity during peak heat hours. Some cities mandate employers provide cooling breaks, drinking water, and shade. Outreach through workers’ unions and informal networks delivers heat safety information. However, economic pressures often force workers to continue despite dangerous conditions, addressing heat vulnerability requires not just individual behavior change but systemic changes ensuring workers’ livelihoods don’t depend on exposing themselves to dangerous heat. Q: Is city heat action plan implementation India increasing or declining? A: Increasing but insufficient. More cities are adopting plans, but rate of expansion lags behind heat wave intensification. Climate change acceleration necessitates faster implementation scaling. Organizations like the University of Toronto India Foundation supporting research and capacity building aim to accelerate expansion, but municipal resource constraints and competing priorities slow progress. Political will at state and national levels remains critical for ensuring heat planning receives sustained priority and funding. As the heat waves become more intense in India, the implementation of action plans for the control of heat waves has emerged as an important part of public health interventions. The figures for urban temperature levels reach 45°C in many cities, with the heat island effect pushing the temperature levels in urban areas by 5-8°C. High temperatures can contribute to both increased mortality during extreme heat events and chronic health conditions resulting from prolonged exposure, with informal workers, elderly citizens, and socio-economically disenfranchised communities being particularly vulnerable. Some cities of India start taking proactive measures against high temperature events rather than passively waiting for them; these include systematized identification of vulnerable populations and creation of the cooling infrastructure which should allow for early warning systems and coordination of efforts made by different sectors. What Are Heat Action Plans? Heat action plans are comprehensive municipal strategies addressing extreme heat through preparedness, mitigation, and response components. Effective plans include heat vulnerability mapping identifying neighborhoods and populations at highest risk; early warning systems alerting residents to dangerous conditions; cooling centers providing refuge; modified work schedules for outdoor laborers; healthcare system preparedness for heat-related illness surge; and long-term infrastructure investment in heat mitigation through green infrastructure, cool roofs, and improved housing. Unlike emergency response plans addressing single events, heat action plans recognize heat as a recurring seasonal challenge requiring proactive, sustained management. This systematic approach differs substantially from traditional municipal operations treating heat as inevitable reality rather than manageable hazard. Leading Cities: Implementation Models Ahmedabad’s Pioneering Approach Ahmedabad initiated the heat action planning process in India in 2013 by engaging in systematic planning. around: Jalgaon’s ‘Heat Action Plan’ Shows Results As White Roof Coating Lowers Indoor Temperatures Free Press Journal e-Paper Get App Home Mumbai News FPJ Shorts Entertainment Bollywood Hollywood Television Regional Film News Movie Reviews Business Technology Games Features Weekend Lifestyle India Sports SportVot Viral Education Study Abroad Tech --> Home Pune Jalgaon’s ‘Heat Action Plan’ Shows Results As White Roof Coating Lowers Indoor Temperatures Jalgaon’s ‘Heat Action Plan’ Shows Results As White Roof Coating Lowers Indoor Temperatures The Corporation selected houses with corrugated iron roofs along Kanalda Road and applied a special solar-reflective white paint to them; observations have shown that this intervention has successfully reduced indoor temperatures by three to four degrees Celsius Vijay Pathak Updated: Friday, March 27, 2026, 03:32 PM IST Jalgaon’s ‘Heat Action Plan’ Shows Results As White Roof Coating Lowers Indoor Temperatures | Sourced (BBC) Jalgaon: While the upper-middle class in the city manages to shield itself from the rising summer temperatures through various means, those living in houses with corrugated iron roofs often face severe hardship. To protect these citizens from the scorching heat, the Jalgaon Municipal Corporation launched a 'Heat Action Plan', and early indications suggest that this initiative is proving to be a success. The Corporation selected houses with corrugated iron roofs along Kanalda Road and applied a special solar-reflective white paint to them; observations have shown that this intervention has successfully reduced indoor temperatures by three to four degrees Celsius. The temperature in Jalgaon city has currently reached 40 degrees Celsius and typically climbs to 45 degrees in May. Today, Jalgaon is gradually transforming into a "jungle of cement and concrete". Comparatively, due to the scarcity of trees within the city, the intensity of the scorching heat is felt much more acutely. Every summer, cases of heatstroke are also reported among the population. To combat the heat, there is currently a surge in the sales of air coolers and air conditioners across the city. Read Also SpiceJet Pune-Delhi Flight Delayed By 4 Hours After Technical Issue, Passengers Deboarded During the afternoons, the streets feel as though an 'unofficial curfew' is in effect, while the city remains heated until late into the night. The common man living in a house with a corrugated iron roof bears the brunt of these extreme temperatures most severely, yet he often possesses no viable alternative to escape it. Taking this situation into account, the Jalgaon Municipal Corporation conducted a survey of the city, which revealed that certain areas experience extremely high temperatures. The survey specifically highlighted that houses with corrugated iron roofs become unbearably hot, exhibiting significantly higher indoor temperatures, prompting the formulation of a comprehensive 'Climate Action Plan'. As part of this plan, a heat-reflective white paint has been applied to houses measuring up to 300 square feet. Initially, 50 houses were selected on a pilot basis to test the efficacy of this initiative. Following the application of solar-reflective white paint to the corrugated metal roofs of houses, tangible results have been observed, with indoor temperatures seen to drop by three to four degrees. Instead of absorbing the sun's rays, this paint reflects them; consequently, the roof's surface does not heat up, and a sense of coolness is maintained within the home. This initiative is now set to be implemented in the city's slum areas. Across the city, many residents, even those with cement-concrete roofs, have begun applying white paint to them. It is reported that this measure is providing them with a measure of relief.
